content: To ensure effective patient care and monitoring, as well as efficient program management, it is essential to establish a structured framework that identifies critical data elements, their sources, users, and intended purposes. This approach enables healthcare managers to ensure that the appropriate data is available at the correct frequency and at the right management levels to support data-driven decision-making. All data collected must have a clear utility, and efforts should be made to simplify the processes of recording and reporting. Data related to HIV prevention, testing, treatment outcomes, and associated infections such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and viral hepatitis can be gathered through various methods. These include routine data reporting from all patients across healthcare facilities, aggregated data from district health information systems, population-based surveys, case surveillance, cohort observations of individuals living with HIV, and periodic evaluations. Additionally, program inputs and processes can be monitored through facility surveys, updated service availability lists, documentation of staff availability and training, and tracking the availability of HIV medicines and diagnostics at different levels of the health system using logistics management information systems. Community-based and community-led service data are also critical. While most routine health information systems (HIS) are facility-based, effective program monitoring and management require data from community-based health services. These services are often delivered through mobile or satellite clinics and by peer or outreach workers. Some services are led and provided by community members to their peers, which is particularly important for key populations facing stigma, discrimination, and criminalization, as they may avoid seeking care at conventional health facilities. Community-led services have proven essential in reaching underserved or marginalized populations. To ensure comprehensive monitoring and integration of community-based and community-led service data into HIS, several considerations are necessary. For example, when community-led organizations provide services, their data systems should be coordinated with those of other service providers, including public, government, and non-community-led NGOs. Data ownership must be clarified, and measures should be implemented to ensure data security and confidentiality for service users. Engaging the community in linking data systems is especially important for populations that frequently experience stigma and discrimination in healthcare settings. Strategically linking unique identifiers (UIDs) for services provided in community-based settings can help avoid double counting of services reported through both community-based and facility-based systems. When collecting key data on HIV programs and responses, it is important to review current monitoring systems, improve linkages with related services (e.g., STIs, TB, viral hepatitis, cervical cancer), and include an integrated set of quality-of-care (QoC) indicators relevant to program management. Evaluations or special surveys may be necessary when routine monitoring systems do not provide sufficient or reliable data. Common data sources include routine health information systems, HIV case surveillance systems, laboratory reporting systems, logistics management information systems, health facility assessments, civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems, and population-based surveys. These surveys can assess service use, behaviors, biomarkers, health outcomes, and trends over time. Special surveys and studies, such as drug resistance surveys and QoC assessments, may also be conducted. Community-led monitoring is vital for understanding successes and failures, as well as assessing determinants, perceptions, values, and experiences of people living with HIV and key populations regarding access to and use of services. Mathematical models can synthesize routine program data, survey data, and population data to estimate outcomes such as new infections, AIDS-related deaths, and the number of people living with HIV. Poor-quality care results in more deaths than lack of access to healthcare, with significant economic losses exceeding $6 trillion annually. Repeated negative experiences with poor-quality or unsafe care can erode trust in health systems, leading to unnecessary suffering and harm. People living with HIV and those accessing HIV-related services deserve high-quality care to achieve and sustain optimal health outcomes. Access alone is insufficient if there are gaps in QoC. Identifying, measuring, and addressing opportunities to improve quality across the care cascade is critical to achieving global targets for ending HIV/AIDS, meeting health-related Sustainable Development Goals, and improving overall health and well-being. QoC is a cross-cutting concept that must be integrated into all aspects of health systems and service delivery to achieve effective outcomes and impact. Health systems are complex, multi-level adaptive networks of interdependent elements, and QoC must be measured across these levels, from service delivery to policy adherence and standards comparison. Increasing interoperability of tools and systems, such as electronic medical records (EMRs) and patient tracking systems, is essential for a systems-level approach that enhances accountability and improves care for individuals seeking HIV services. Measurement is a foundational requirement for quality health services, requiring stakeholders to track service delivery and promote accountability. Collecting strategic information at multiple client-provider interfaces and service delivery points provides visibility into services that can be addressed through quality improvement initiatives. QoC measurement should capture the quality of integrated care for HIV and related infections across multiple service delivery points, using longitudinal client-level data supplemented by other sources. It should also account for the diversity of people seeking HIV services, employing safe data collection and analysis strategies to explore and analyze this diversity. All data used to measure the quality of HIV services must be anonymized or de-identified and securely stored. The first step in the QoC process is to determine the availability and adequacy of national, subnational, or program indicators and data for QoC measurement. Mechanisms to share QoC findings and adapt service approaches based on data and implementation experience are key. While routine data and existing tools should be the primary sources, additional approaches may be warranted to gather data on patient experiences and satisfaction not captured through routine programmatic data. Qualitative methods may be necessary to collect and analyze patient and healthcare worker experiences. Person-centered measurement and monitoring systems should include tools such as questionnaires to assess patient perceptions and satisfaction with integrated care. Validated measures and tools should be used when available. Focus group discussions can gather in-depth information from patients and their families about their experiences with services and validate tools for measuring satisfaction. These discussions should be conducted in coordination with trusted stakeholders, such as peer groups or community-based organizations, to foster open and respectful dialogue.
